action_criteria.expected_evidence: Right frontoparietal 5.8 cm mass centred in the precentral gyrus with thick irregular nodular ring enhancement, central necrosis, rim restricted diffusion, extensive vasogenic edema, 9 mm midline shift and early subfalcine herniation
action_criteria.label: Order MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast (tumor protocol with DWI, FLAIR, post-contrast T1) to characterize the right frontoparietal lesion, define mass effect, and plan surgery
action_criteria.rationale: Contrast MRI with a standardised tumour protocol characterises the lesion and its mass effect, identifies the target for tissue sampling and is required before surgery (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: rCBV ratio 5.2 in the enhancing rim, supporting a high-grade neoplasm and identifying the target for tissue sampling
action_criteria.label: Order MR perfusion imaging (DSC perfusion) to assess tumor vascularity and target highest-grade region for biopsy
action_criteria.rationale: Elevated rCBV supports a high-grade neoplasm and points to the most vascular region to sample; tissue decides the diagnosis (Law 2003).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Cho/NAA ratio 14.0 with prominent lipid and lactate peaks in the enhancing component, supporting a high-grade neoplasm
action_criteria.label: Order MR spectroscopy (1H-MRS) to characterize tumor metabolic profile
action_criteria.rationale: A raised Cho/NAA ratio with lipid and lactate supports a high-grade neoplasm; it does not replace tissue (Bulik 2013).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Lateralized periodic discharges at 1 to 1.5 Hz over F4 and C4 with right frontoparietal polymorphic delta slowing; no electrographic seizures recorded

action_criteria.rationale: After a first seizure with a large hemispheric tumour, an EEG identifies periodic discharges or ongoing electrographic seizures that call for continuous monitoring and escalation of antiseizure treatment. EEG does not diagnose the tumour.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No extracranial primary malignancy or metastatic disease
action_criteria.label: Order contrast CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis if a solitary metastasis remains on the differential
action_criteria.rationale: Body staging is optional when a single necrotic infiltrative mass in a young adult without a cancer history favours a primary glioma.

action_criteria.rationale: Platelets, coagulation and a type and screen must be known before a neurosurgical procedure, and baseline glucose and electrolytes on dexamethasone.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform lumbar puncture: 9 mm midline shift with early subfalcine herniation and papilledema carries a risk of herniation
Do not initiate definitive tumor-directed therapy (radiation, temozolomide, alkylating chemotherapy) before tissue diagnosis is established
Do not start therapeutic anticoagulation without a clear thromboembolic indication, given upcoming neurosurgical intervention and bleeding risk
required_recommendations: Refer urgently to neurosurgery for maximal safe resection of the right frontoparietal lesion, with preoperative functional MRI and DTI tractography and intraoperative mapping; send the specimen for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis (WHO CNS5).

Continue dexamethasone, started in the emergency department, for symptomatic vasogenic oedema at the lowest effective dose (for example 4 mg every 6 to 8 hours while mass effect is marked), with glucose monitoring and gastric protection, and taper after surgery.

Continue levetiracetam, started in the emergency department, for the documented focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure of left arm onset; this is treatment of tumour-related epilepsy, not prophylaxis. Review the dose against seizure control and tolerance. Avoid enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital), which lower dexamethasone and chemotherapy exposure and the efficacy of her contraceptive.
Continue EEG monitoring given LPDs after a first seizure, and escalate antiseizure treatment if electrographic seizures appear.

Withhold the combined oral contraceptive around surgery (major neurosurgery and a high-grade glioma both raise venous thromboembolism risk) with mechanical thromboprophylaxis, and arrange a non-oestrogen method, since effective contraception is needed during temozolomide.

After the integrated diagnosis, refer to the neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team; for glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, at age 31 with KPS 80, radiotherapy 60 Gy in 30 fractions with concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide (Stupp 2005; EANO 2021), with fertility counselling before treatment and Pneumocystis prophylaxis during the concomitant phase by an agent other than trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole because of her sulfonamide allergy.

differential.key_features: IDH-mutant astrocytoma is the commoner high-grade astrocytoma at 31; IDH1 R132H IHC negative, IDH1/IDH2 sequencing wildtype and ATRX retained exclude it
A hemispheric IDH-wildtype glioma in a young adult raises it; no H3 G34 mutation on sequencing, and TERT mutation with +7/-10 define glioblastoma
No cancer history; staging CT negative; a single necrotic infiltrative mass favours a primary glioma, and tissue is glial
Immunocompetent lymphoma is usually homogeneously enhancing with diffuse restricted diffusion and no necrosis; thick ring enhancement with necrosis and a glial histology exclude it
No fever or leukocytosis; restricted diffusion at the enhancing rim rather than centrally, and markedly elevated rim rCBV; tissue shows tumour
Thick closed ring enhancement, marked mass effect and central necrosis are atypical for tumefactive demyelination, which usually shows an incomplete ring; tissue shows tumour

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Priya Nair is a 31-year-old right-handed woman with a history of infrequent migraines who presents to the emergency department after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure. She reports that over the past six weeks, she has been experiencing headaches that are qualitatively different from her usual migraines: they are constant, dull, pressure-like, and worst upon awakening in the morning, sometimes accompanied by nausea. Sumatriptan, which previously controlled her migraines effectively, has had no effect on these new headaches. Over the past three weeks, she noticed progressive difficulty with her left hand, initially manifesting as clumsiness when typing on her keyboard and difficulty manipulating small objects. Her partner confirms that the left-hand weakness has been worsening steadily and that she has been dropping items more frequently. She also describes feeling more fatigued than usual and has had two episodes of nausea with vomiting over the past week, occurring in the morning without clear provocation. She denies any visual changes, speech difficulties, sensory loss, bowel or bladder dysfunction, fever, weight loss, night sweats, or recent infections. She has no history of malignancy, no prior seizures, and no recent travel. This morning, while sitting at her desk, she experienced rhythmic jerking of her left arm followed by a generalized convulsion witnessed by her partner, who called emergency services. She was postictal and drowsy for approximately twenty minutes. A non-contrast CT scan obtained in the emergency department demonstrated a large hyperdense mass in the right frontoparietal region with surrounding hypodensity and approximately 9 mm of midline shift to the left. She was started on intravenous dexamethasone and levetiracetam and admitted to the neurology service for further evaluation.
